title: Best single trade
statement:
You have the closing price of a collectible for each day in `prices`. You may buy it on one day and sell it on a later day, once.

Return the largest profit you can make. If no trade makes money, return 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must I buy before I sell?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, the sell day must come after the buy day.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Rules out simply subtracting the minimum from the maximum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I make more than one trade?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, exactly one buy and one sell, or no trade.
clarifyingQuestions.why: Separates this from the many-trades variant.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if no trade is profitable, or there are fewer than two days?

edgeCases.why: The global minimum comes after the global maximum, so max minus min is wrong.

approaches.name: Every pair
approaches.idea: For each buy day, check every later sell day.

approaches.name: Track the lowest price so far
approaches.idea: Walk the days once, remembering the lowest price seen. Each day, the best sale today is today’s price minus that lowest price.

optimal.name: Running minimum
optimal.explanation: Keep lowest = the minimum price so far and best = 0. For each price, update lowest, then best = max(best, price - lowest). Updating lowest first is fine because selling on the same day gives a profit of 0.

hintLadder: If you had to sell today, which day would you have wanted to buy?
Do you need to look back over every earlier day to know that?
What single number summarizes the past for this question?
Track the lowest price so far and compare each day against it.

expectedMentions.what: Confirms the buy must come before the sell
Proposes tracking the lowest price so far for O(n)
Explains why max minus min is wrong when the minimum comes later

followUps: You may make any number of trades, holding at most one item at a time.
Each trade has a fixed fee.

referenceSolution.python:
def best_trade(prices):
    lowest = float('inf')
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best

walkthrough.say: I have to buy before I sell, and only once, right? If nothing makes money I return zero?
Brute force compares every buy day with every later sell day, n squared.
If I sell on a given day, the best buy is the lowest price before it. So I just keep a running minimum and, each day, compare today’s price to it. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.
I can’t just take the overall max minus the overall min, because the minimum might come after the maximum.
Two variables. I update the minimum first; selling the same day just gives zero.
walkthrough.code:
def best_trade(prices):
    lowest = float('inf')
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best

walkthrough.say: For 8, 3, 6, 2, 9, 4: the minimum goes 8, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, and the best goes 0, 0, 3, 3, 7, 7. Answer 7, buying at 2 and selling at 9.
For 2, 10, 1, 4: best becomes 8 at day 2. Later the minimum drops to 1, but 4 minus 1 is only 3, so 8 stays. Max minus min would have said 9, which isn’t a legal trade.
